transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-08-09
Start: 16:30 UTC
Duration: ~56 minutes
Attendees: Alicia Park (Redwood AE), Devon Li (Redwood SE), Marco Ruiz (PivotalLedger - Platform Eng), Lisa Chen (PivotalLedger - SRE), Nadia Karim (PivotalLedger - Head of AI)

Summary: quick demo of API key hierarchy, org vs project keys, and traffic-shaping controls in Console + Optimize. Discussed rate limiting strategies, quota assignment, failover routing, and security/compliance questions. Agreed on pilot and benchmark run.

Topics: API key hierarchy; token-bucket vs leaky-bucket shaping; per-project quotas; sticky routing for model variants; Dedicated vs Hosted tradeoffs; security (KMS, SOC2, audit logs); billing segmentation.

Transcript:
[00:00] Alicia Park: hey everyone, thanks for joining. uh we'll try to keep this to under an hour, quick intros— i'm Alicia, AE on the infra team. Devon's gonna walk through the console and the traffic shaping bits.
[00:14] Marco Ruiz: hi Alicia, Marco here. we manage platform infra at PivotalLedger. Lisa and Nadia here as well.
[00:19] Lisa Chen: hi all.
[00:21] Nadia Karim: hey.
[00:23] Devon Li: hey team, thanks. so first slide, uh, quick context: you mentioned you have multiple product teams hitting the same Redwood org and you want predictable per-team SLOs plus cost controls, is that right?
[00:34] Marco Ruiz: yes correct. we have three internal teams, prod-trade, risk, and insights. they all call the same model endpoints right now which is messy. we want per-team quotas, a way to do burst capacity, and to route to cheaper quantized variants for non-critical calls.
[00:48] Devon Li: perfect. that maps to the org/project key pattern—so you create an org, then create project keys per team. each key can have a quota policy, concurrency and burst allowances, and sticky routing rules. i'll share my screen. sorry, slight delay.
[01:04] [screen share noise]
[01:12] Devon Li: okay, console on screen—on the left you'll see Projects. here's prod-trade's project key. you can see rate limits configured as token-bucket per minute and per-second windows, with an additional concurrency cap.
[01:28] Lisa Chen: quick question, do you support leaky-bucket shaping? some of our services do token-bucket but others want smoothing to avoid spikes.
[01:36] Devon Li: great question. under the hood we support both shaping modes. token-bucket is default for burst handling; we also have a leaky-bucket style lane which enforces a steady drain rate. in Optimize you can run a simulation against your traffic profile to see tail latency impact.
[01:49] Marco Ruiz: nice. and the sticky routing you mentioned—how do we ensure risk team always goes to low-latency nodes?
[01:56] Devon Li: two levers—priority lanes and pinned variants. Priority lanes let you set 'low-latency' lane that favors high-tier hardware and model variants. Pinned variants let you bind a project key to a particular model family or quant level, so risk can be pinned to FP16 on Dedicated. The system will still fall back if capacity is exhausted, based on your fallback policy.
[02:15] Nadia Karim: oh, fallback policy—what's the chain look like? e.g., prefer fp16 -> int8 -> hosted cheap variant?
[02:22] Devon Li: exactly. you can configure a fallback list with routing priorities and cost overrides. Example: prefer rwdx-fp16, then rwdx-quantized-int8, then hosted-open-compat as last resort. you can also set SLO thresholds that trigger an automatic switch.
[02:36] Lisa Chen: and billing—if we use a hosted fallback, does the cost appear mixed in the same invoice? we need clear cost centers per project.
[02:43] Alicia Park: yes, billing tags propagate by project key. you get token-level cost attribution per-project. the console export includes per-route and per-model breakdowns so finance can reconcile.
[02:52] Marco Ruiz: good. can you show an example quota policy? we want monthly budget caps and per-minute throttles.
[02:58] Devon Li: sure — open Policy -> Quotas. here's a policy bound to the insights project: monthly token cap 10M, per-minute 200k, concurrency 50. you can also set soft vs hard caps—soft caps emit warnings and enact a graceful slowdown; hard caps return 429.
[03:17] Marco Ruiz: graceful slowdown—what does that look like? is it queueing? 503?
[03:21] Devon Li: SLO-aware graceful fallback: we can either delay responses (up to configured latency budget), route to cache hits if prefix matched, or degrade model (move to cheaper variant). if configured to queue, it will hold for up to X ms and then return 429 if still not served. Queueing is bounded to protect the runtime.
[03:38] Nadia Karim: i like cache + degrade rather than just 429. can we keep a small KV cache for recent prompts?
[03:44] Devon Li: yes, prefix caching and KV cache for embeddings/kv-style responses is supported — configurable per-project. Optimize will recommend which prompts are good candidates for prefix caching.
[03:54] Lisa Chen: security question: when a project key is issued, where is it stored and how do we rotate it? we need KMS/HSM integration and audit logs.
[04:02] Alicia Park: keys are stored encrypted via customer-managed KMS integration for Private customers, and Redwood-managed KMS for Hosted. rotation can be automated via the console with staged key rollout—old key remains valid for a window. and all key actions produce audit entries with request metadata. we also support SSO/SAML and RBAC.
[04:19] Marco Ruiz: for our compliance we need SOC2 attestation and a PCI/PII data flow map — can you share relevant docs?
[04:25] Alicia Park: absolutely. i'll attach our SOC2 report and a whitepaper on data residency and flow. for Private deployments we can provide an on-prem artifact and HSM integration notes.
[04:34] Nadia Karim: curious about multi-tenant isolation—if two projects share the same GPU pool on Dedicated, any risk of cache or KV leaks across projects?
[04:43] Devon Li: isolation is enforced at the runtime level: KV namespace and prefix cache are per-project when you enable project scoping. shared GPU pools are multi-tenant at compute level but we enforce memory and KV isolation. for extra separation you can pin to dedicated pool nodes.
[04:58] Marco Ruiz: sounds good. can you walk through an example traffic shaping policy for prod-trade which has spiky usage?
[05:05] Devon Li: sure. example: prod-trade gets a token-bucket per-second of 2000 TPS with a 10k token burst; concurrency cap 100; backlog queue 2000 ms; fallback to quantized variants for non-essential endpoints. Also we attach an autoscale policy to the pool for scheduled spikes.
[05:24] Lisa Chen: autoscale—how fast can it respond? we need to ensure the SLOs for trade are met.
[05:29] Devon Li: autoscale depends on the underlying Dedicated config—burst capacity can be configured to bring up pre-warmed nodes within 90s for warm pools. For cold pockets it's longer. Our routing also allows temporary over-provision from Hosted to cover short gaps.
[05:42] Marco Ruiz: you mentioned Optimize earlier—what recommendations does it provide for quantization vs latency trade-offs?
[05:48] Devon Li: Optimize analyzes request distributions, sequence lengths, and latency sensitivity. It will suggest quantization profiles per endpoint—e.g., insights/chat -> int8 with higher tolerance; risk -> fp16. It also suggests batching windows and KV cache thresholds. There's a confidence score and predicted cost savings per suggestion.
[06:06] Lisa Chen: can Optimize be run against historical traffic? we have month of logs.
[06:10] Devon Li: yep, you can upload a traffic trace or connect to S3 logs. we run a simulation and give a report. note: anonymize prompts if needed for privacy.
[06:18] Nadia Karim: any gotchas with model fallbacks and safety? sometimes different variants have slightly different output distributions which could affect downstream features.
[06:26] Devon Li: totally, and that's why we support eval sets and a canary rollout flow. You can add prompt-based unit tests; if metric drift exceeds threshold we failover to a safe variant. Also you can pin safety-critical endpoints to non-quantized variants.
[06:39] Marco Ruiz: okay real world—if we set monthly cap and one team hit it unexpectedly, can we auto-bill overages or do we prefer throttles?
[06:48] Alicia Park: flexible—billing overages are a commercial setting. Most customers prefer throttles and alerting where finance receives notification and can approve overage windows. We'll show billing thresholds alerts in the console demo.
[07:00] [screen pause while Alicia pulls up billing page]
[07:08] Devon Li: switching to demo of policy bindings: here you can bind a quota policy to an org or to an individual project key. binding at project-key level overrides org-level defaults. you can also define inheritance rules.
[07:22] Lisa Chen: inheritance rules? like child projects inherit caps unless overridden?
[07:26] Devon Li: exactly. useful for onboarding new teams with baseline limits.
[07:31] Marco Ruiz: i see a field for route-specific quotas—we have heavy embedding endpoints vs chat endpoints, can we split quotas by endpoint?
[07:39] Devon Li: yes, per-route quotas and per-model quotas. You can also weight tokens differently (embeddings counted as X tokens) and apply separate monthly budgets.
[07:49] Nadia Karim: how do we test policies before prod? do you have a sandbox?
[07:53] Devon Li: we recommend creating a staging org with mirrored projects. there's a policy dry-run mode that logs what would have happened. Optimize can run simulations too.
[08:02] Marco Ruiz: okay, let's talk pilot scope—we want to validate that our rate shaping holds under trade-day peaks. what's the best approach?
[08:09] Devon Li: recommended: 1) create dev org with project keys for prod-trade and risk; 2) provide a traffic trace to Devon; 3) Devon runs a 2-hour benchmark with increasing load to target qps and intersperse cold/warm caches; 4) capture latency and fallback stats -> produce a runbook with suggested quota tweaks.
[08:26] Marco Ruiz: perfect, we'll provide traces.
[08:29] Lisa Chen: slight tangent—SSO mapping: can we map org/project keys to our IdP groups?
[08:34] Alicia Park: yes, RBAC integrates with SAML groups so project keys can be provisioned by role.
[08:39] Nadia Karim: anything about data residency? some of our models touch EU-only data.
[08:43] Alicia Park: yes, region routing can be scoped by project. For Private customers we can enforce VPC-only egress. We'll include region and residency documentation.
[08:53] Marco Ruiz: one more technical question—how do you compute per-token costs for mixed model fallbacks? is there an attribution model?
[08:59] Devon Li: attribution is done per-inference event: we record actual model variant served and tokens consumed. If fallback occurs mid-stream, tokens are split between variants. Billing exports contain token-level records you can join to cost model.
[09:12] Lisa Chen: good. also curious about concurrency limits—we have a few latency-sensitive RPCs, if concurrency cap hits and requests queue, how do we surface that to the caller?
[09:21] Devon Li: the API returns structured error codes and headers that indicate quota state and a retry-after. We also emit real-time metrics and traces you can subscribe to and send to your observability platform.
[09:33] Marco Ruiz: okay thanks. can we look at a sample policy JSON?
[09:37] Devon Li: sure — here's a sample: {"policy_name":"prod-trade-shape","per_second":2000,"burst":10000,"concurrency":100,"fallback":["fp16","int8","hosted-compat"],"backlog_ms":2000} — apologies, transcription may garble braces.
[09:59] Nadia Karim: looks straightforward. two quick followups: 1) do you support per-customer rate limiting vs per-project? we have some external tenants too; 2) can we tier SLA per key?
[10:10] Devon Li: yes to both. Per-customer is supported by binding policies to org or custom attributes (like tenant_id). SLA tiers are implemented via policy labels—gold/silver/bronze—affecting routing priority and autoscale settings.
[10:22] Marco Ruiz: what's the uplift cost to get gold routing?
[10:25] Alicia Park: uplift depends on Dedicated capacity commitment. we'll send a tailored pricing sheet but generally gold routing implies reserved pool capacity and higher per-token rate for guaranteed latency.
[10:35] Lisa Chen: can you demo the alerts and the cost dashboard?
[10:38] Devon Li: switching to cost dashboard — you can filter by project, model, route, and timeframe. top contributors, forecasted spend, and alert rules are here. you can create alerts for token burn rate or forecast vs budget.
[10:52] Marco Ruiz: nice. is there a webhook for alerts?
[10:55] Devon Li: yes, alert destinations include webhook, Slack, PagerDuty, and email.
[11:00] Alicia Park: quick pause — any other compliance or technical blockers we should call out?
[11:04] Lisa Chen: just around network egress for Private. we'll want a diagram of the VPC setup.
[11:08] Alicia Park: okay will include.
[11:10] Nadia Karim: on evaluation, we need to validate quality impact from quantized fallbacks. hope you can help with a small eval harness.
[11:16] Devon Li: yes we'll run the canary and eval. we'll set up prompt-based tests and quality metrics.
[11:22] Marco Ruiz: timeline—if we start pilot mid-August can we get results by end of August?
[11:28] Devon Li: yes, 2-week pilot + analysis; target wrap-up by 2027-08-31 is feasible.
[11:35] Alicia Park: great. let's recap next steps.
[11:38] Alicia Park: action items: (1) Alicia send SOC2 and KMS brief; (2) Devon to run benchmark and share runbook; (3) Marco provide traffic traces and SLOs; (4) Alicia send pricing. We'll aim to provision test keys by next Tue.
[11:54] Marco Ruiz: sounds good. thanks everyone.
[11:58] Lisa Chen: thanks.
[12:00] Nadia Karim: thanks all.

End of transcript.
